title: Building one tiny workshop exposed my lazy UV workflow
author: med_yasss
selftext:
For a small game set in a one-room repair shop, I needed enough props to stop the room feeling like a gray box. The first batch was a stool, toolbox, wall cabinet, oil can, and a chunky work lamp. Keeping the shapes simple was intentional because I wanted to spend my time arranging the room, not polishing one hero asset.



Early passes stayed rough while I cleaned the geometry and exported the pieces before bringing them into the engine. For texturing, I inspected each UV layout instead of assuming a nice viewport render meant the asset was ready.



The cabinet was where my UV inspection became important. Its front looked consistent, but the painted scratch on its side ran backwards across a seam, and a directional checker confirmed the island behind it was mirrored. Like the other props, that cabinet began as a text-to-3D model from meshy; after import, I ran my normal UV cleanup on it like anything else I bring in. I compared island orientation, texel density, and directional textures across the set, then unmirrored that island and repacked the cabinet. My repack scaled its islands up, so the cabinet ended up reading sharper than the stool beside it, a mismatch I created myself while fixing the seam.



My current workflow is generation, silhouette cleanup, UV check, texture check under plain lighting, export, then a quick in-engine pass at the actual camera distance.



I only noticed the mismatch once the props were together in the room. Do you check texel density across a whole set before import?

comments.author: Fair_Engineering_480
comments.body: After using AI texturing in meshy on a batch of props, I started checking both density and seams with a directional UV checker. On your cabinet, I would look for arrows flipping across the mirrored island and compare square size against the stool. That puts the mirror problem and the density mismatch in the same diagnostic pass.
